name: Pazhamudircholai Murugan Temple
deity: Murugan, worshipped with Valli and Deivanai
tradition: Kaumaram, the worship of Murugan within the Shaiva tradition
period: Ancient grove shrine, sung in Sangam poetry
summary: Sixth and last of Murugan’s six abodes, Pazhamudircholai crowns a wooded hill near Madurai — a forest grove shrine where the god is worshipped with both his consorts, Valli and Deivanai.

sections.history: Pazhamudircholai lies on Solaimalai, a wooded hill among the Alagar range northeast of Madurai, beside the Vaishnava shrine of Alagar. It is the abode with which the Sangam-era Tirumurugatruppadai, the ancient guide-poem to Murugan’s shrines, comes to its close, and it has been revered as the sixth and culminating abode since early times. A grove rather than a grand tower, it keeps something of the old forest sanctity of Murugan worship, close to the springs and greenery of the hill.
sections.architecture: True to its name — cholai, a grove; pazham, ripe fruit — the temple sits amid trees on the hillside, a modest shrine framed by forest rather than by soaring gopurams. Murugan is worshipped here with both Valli and Deivanai at his side, a rare completeness among the six abodes. Nearby lie the Noopura Ganga spring and the older Alagar temple below, so that a visit weaves together grove, water, and the green slopes of the Alagar hills.
sections.legends: Pazhamudircholai is bound to the beloved story of the poetess Avvaiyar. Resting beneath a fruit tree, she was asked by a cowherd boy whether she wanted “roasted” or “unroasted” fruit; puzzled, she found the boy playing with words on the ripe naval fruit, and realised she had been humbled in wit by Murugan himself in disguise. The tale, cherished across the Tamil land, marks this grove as the abode where the god teaches humility to the wise, and where devotion outreaches learning.
sections.festivals: Vaikasi Visakam, the god’s birth star, Skanda Sashti, and Thai Poosam draw pilgrims up the hill, and the temple shares in the festival life of the neighbouring Alagar shrine. As the closing abode of the Arupadai Veedu, it receives many who complete the six-temple pilgrimage here. Kavadi and abhishekam mark the season, and the grove fills with families who climb for darshan and linger by the spring.
sections.experience: Reaching Pazhamudircholai is a journey into green: the road climbs through the Alagar hills to a grove where birdsong and the rustle of leaves surround the shrine. After the grandeur of the other abodes, its forest simplicity is a quiet culmination — many who have travelled the six abodes feel the pilgrimage complete here, among trees and spring water. Pilgrims often pause at the Noopura Ganga and the Alagar temple below, so that the visit gathers the god of the hills, his consorts, and the living forest into one unhurried close.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 6:00 am to 1:00 pm and 3:00 pm to 8:00 pm daily; hours may vary with the hill road and extend during festivals.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — dhotis or trousers for men, sarees or salwar kameez for women, shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the stands outside.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted around the sanctum; follow posted rules and staff guidance, especially during festivals.
visit.gettingThere: Pazhamudircholai is about 25 km northeast of Madurai on the Alagar hills, reached by road via Alagar Koyil; Madurai has the nearest railway junction and airport, and local buses serve the hill.
